speaker: Karri Saarinen
title: Inside Linear: Building with taste, craft, and focus | Karri Saarinen
question: In B2B productivity software, why does making a tool highly flexible and configurable often hurt team productivity?
guest: I personally believe that productivity software, and especially company software, should be opinionated. What productivity software is trying to do is make people productive—meaning you actually do something that matters for the company, like building a feature, fixing something, or designing something that provides value for the customer. There's this notion that flexible software is great, and it can be sometimes. But what happens is people start spending a lot of time figuring things out. If you can use a feature in ten different ways, then every person or every team figures out a different way of doing it. Our thinking is to provide good defaults and good opinions—this is how the feature works and this is how the workflow works—so you don't have to think about it and can focus on your actual work. My design mantra is always to design something for someone. It's very hard to design everything for everyone because you just end up with a generalized solution. The value of being opinionated is that you don't spend more time on the tool than on your actual work.

points.core: High configurability diverts time from customer-facing work toward figuring out the tool itself.
points.note: Accept: users spend effort designing or tweaking tool setup instead of building features or shipping value. Do not credit: generic complaints that complex UIs are confusing.

points.core: Allowing many usage paths causes different teams to invent incompatible internal workflows.
points.note: Accept: open-ended features lead individuals or teams to configure conflicting ways of working, fragmenting coordination. Do not credit: generic statements about 'lack of alignment' without linking to multi-way tool flexibility.

points.core: Designing for every possible use case produces a generalized, poorly optimized experience.
points.note: Accept: trying to build everything for everyone sacrifices optimized defaults for a specific target workflow. Do not credit: vague platitudes like 'focus on your target user'.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Flexibility shifts the burden of design from the vendor to the team, and most teams are not good at, or paid for, designing their own workflows.

A highly configurable tool ships without an opinion about how work should be done, so every team must first decide how to structure it: which fields, statuses, views, and conventions to use. That setup and its ongoing maintenance are real work that displaces the actual job, and it often becomes a form of procrastination that feels productive.

The bigger cost is coordination. Collaboration depends on shared conventions, and flexibility lets each person or team build their own. The result is fragmentation: inconsistent structures, duplicated information, and nobody sure where things live or which version is authoritative. Onboarding gets harder because newcomers must learn the homegrown system, not just the tool, and that system usually depends on one or two people who built it and decays when they leave.

Opinionated tools, by contrast, embed tested practices as defaults, so teams trade some fit for speed, consistency, and lower cognitive load. Flexibility pays off mainly when a team has unusual needs and someone accountable for maintaining the setup.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Highly flexible B2B tools shift the burden of workflow design from the software vendor onto the customer, turning everyday coordination into unproductive "meta-work." Instead of executing tasks, teams spend hours debating schemas, custom fields, and folder hierarchies while maintaining brittle configurations as the organization evolves.

Without opinionated defaults, different sub-teams inevitably invent incompatible conventions, which fragments shared context, breaks cross-functional reporting, and makes collaboration harder rather than easier. At the individual level, excessive configurability increases cognitive load and decision fatigue: routine actions like logging an issue or sharing an update require deciding where information belongs and how to structure it, slowing daily momentum and steepening onboarding for new hires. Over time, ungoverned flexibility breeds clutter and administrative debt, leaving employees unsure which views, statuses, or documents are authoritative—and often driving reluctant teammates back to ad-hoc spreadsheets or chat threads. Opinionated software boosts productivity precisely by settling these recurring structural choices up front so teams can focus on the work itself rather than managing the tool.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Flexibility moves design work from the vendor onto the customer, and most teams are bad at that work and don't have time for it. A rigid tool comes with an opinion about how work should flow. A blank-canvas tool makes every team invent its own workflows, fields, statuses and conventions, and the result usually depends on whoever set it up first.

That causes several problems that build on each other. Teams lose time debating setup ("bikeshedding") instead of doing the work. Each team configures things differently, so cross-team visibility, reporting and handoffs break down because "done" or "priority" means something different in each workspace. Configurations pile up over time as custom fields, automations and exceptions accumulate until nobody understands the system and new hires face a steep learning curve. Many choices also raise cognitive load for everyone who uses the tool, not just the admin.

This is why opinionated products like Linear or Basecamp often beat endlessly customizable ones like Jira or Notion setups on team speed. Good defaults spread best practices and keep people consistent, so users can focus on the work instead of the tool.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Highly configurable B2B tools often hurt team productivity because flexibility shifts the burden of workflow design from the software vendor onto the team. Instead of doing core work, employees spend time debating schemas, tweaking permissions, and maintaining custom setups—turning the tool itself into ongoing meta-work.

Flexibility also erodes shared conventions. When every department or manager can structure boards, fields, and statuses differently, the organization loses a common language. Cross-team handoffs break down, reporting becomes unreliable, and new hires face steep onboarding friction because they must learn a bespoke internal system rather than an intuitive standard. Over time, small ad-hoc customizations accumulate into cluttered, brittle workspaces that create decision fatigue and slow routine actions. Paradoxically, when software lacks opinionated guardrails, teams often lose trust in the system and revert to informal side channels like spreadsheets and chat, defeating the tool's original purpose.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
A highly configurable tool makes teams spend time designing and maintaining the way they work. Someone has to choose fields, statuses, permissions, and automations. Everyone else has to learn those choices and keep up as they change.

The bigger cost shows up when teams work together. If two departments use different definitions of “done,” a handoff can stall or a shared report can mislead. Each department may have a setup that works well for it, while the company spends more time reconciling those setups.

Strong defaults give people a shared way to start. Flexibility pays off when it solves a recurring problem that’s costly enough to justify the extra setup, training, and maintenance.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Flexibility can make each person’s work easier while making the team’s work harder to coordinate. If everyone can define their own statuses, views, and workflows, one person’s “done” might mean ready for review while another’s means ready for the customer. A teammate taking over a task then has to ask what the status means before acting on it. Even when everyone uses the same setup, the team still spends time choosing, teaching, and maintaining it.

Good defaults and a few shared conventions let people make routine decisions once and rely on them across handoffs. Customization pays off when it solves a recurring problem whose cost exceeds the effort of setting up and sustaining a different way of working.
